full_judgment:
A. T. M. Masud. J.—This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca, and the complainant opposite-party to show cause why the proceedings against the petitioners in Criminal Case No. 42 of 1974 pending in the 1st Labour Court of Bangladesh at Dacca should not be quashed. 

 5. The Union raised industrial dispute against JP SC in 1973 and the said dispute was referred to the 1st Labour Court of Bangladesh at Dacca by the Government for adjudication under the provisions of Industrial Relations Ordinance, 1969. The Labour Court by its judgment dated 28.2.74 in I. R Case No. 99 of 1973 passed the following award: 

 "That the case be allowed on contest in part without costs. The workers of the R. Sim Jute Press are declared to be employees of the R, Sim Jute Press. Workers putting in requisite period of service be made permanent and leave facilities be made available to them as are admissible under the relevant laws. The demand for minimum wages and arrears be rejected. 

 7. On 13.9.74 complainant opposite party filed a case being Criminal Case No. 42 of 1974 in the 1st Labour Court of Bangladesh at Dacca under the provisions of section 55 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance against the petitioners alleging wilful refusal to implement the Award. Summons was issued and the petitioners appeared in the Labour Court. 

 9. JPSC therefore filed Misc. Case No. 84 of 1974 under section 50 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance before the Labour Acrenate Tribunal for interpretation of the expression "Three years continuous service" as used in the Award and during the pendency of the case further proceedings of Criminal Case No. 42 of 1974 was stayed by the Labour Court at the instance of the petitioners. 

 13. On 10.5.76 the Chairman of the Labour Court vacated the Stay Order in Criminal Case No. 42 of 1974 on the prayer of the complainant opposite party and liked date for hearing which was, however, adjourned on the prayer of the complainant. 

 14. On 24.5.76 petitioner No. 1 filed a petition for dismissal of the case before the Labour Court on the ground, inter alia, that no date for implementation of the Award having been mentioned in the Award and the Award having been implemented on 15.5.76 the case was not maintainable but the learned Chairman of the Labour Court did not pass any order on the said petition. 

 16. The Labour Court trying an offence under the Industrial Relations Ordinance has got the power of a Magistrate, 1st Class, and he can take cognizance of an offence on receipt of a complaint. Since there is nothing in the Ordinance to indicate that only a person affected by the offence can lodge the complaint, any person having knowledge of the commission of an offence may set the law in motion by a complaint even though he is not personally interested or affected by the offence. In the instant case, however, the complainant was admittedly a Member and General Secretary of the Union when the Labour Court took cognizance of the offence on his complaint. We, therefore, find no substance in the aforesaid contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

 18. On a perusal of the Memorandum and Articles of Association, it arrears that the Corporation is a joint stock company within the meaning of the Companies Act, major Shareholders being the Government. The materials placed before us are not sufficient to hold that in the facts and circumstances of the case petitioner No. 2 is entitled to get the protection of section 197 Cr.P.C. It further appears that no such point was raised before the Labour Court who was competent to take a decision on the question if necessary after taking evidence. We, are therefore, unable to accept the aforesaid contention of the learned Advocate, It was next argued by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that although it was mandatory under section 40 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance, to specify the date from which the Award would be effective and the time-limit by which it shall be implemented, neither the Labour Court nor the Labour Appellate Tribunal specified the same. The learned Advocate submitted that as the JPSC took lease of the premises in question in July, 1972, none of the workers did put in three years service with JPSC and as such none of them could be made permanent and for seeking a clarification in the matter the Corporation had to move the Labour Appellate Tribunal under section 50 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. After obtaining clarification in this regard they took necessary steps far implementation of the Award and after obtaining the approval of the Ministry concerned by a notice dated 15. 5.76 the Award was implemented. The learned Advocate, further, submitted that the Corporation had no papers previous to the date of starting the Jute Pros by the Corporation and so they had to request the complainant to furnish list of workers eligible for being made permanent and to furnish papers in support of such claim. Since they did not get the cooperation of the complainant in this regard, after much difficulty they had to collect all particulars necessary for implementing the Award and for the aforesaid reasons the Award could not be promptly implemented. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submitted that there was no wilful failure on the part of the petitioners to implement the Award and as such proceeding under section 55 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance are liable to the quashed for the end of justice. 

 19. Under section 55 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance wilful failure to implement the Award has been made punishable. In the instant case petitioners have implemented the Award and they have furnished sufficient cogent reasons for the delay in implementing the Award. In that view of the matter and particularly when no time limit was mentioned in the Award; it is difficult to hold that petitioners wilfully failed to implement the Award and wilful failure is the most material ingredient of an offence under section 55 of the Industrial Relation Ordinance. 

 20. Having considered the entire facts and circumstances of the case we are of opinion that continuation of the further proceedings against the petitioners will amount to an abuse of the processes of the Court. Accordingly we quash the proceedings of Criminal Case No. 42 of 1974 pending in the 1st Labour Court of Bangladesh at Dacca.
